findings.title: Duplicate React key when a categorical column contains both SQL null and the literal string "__null__"
findings.description: In CategoricalSummaryCard, each distinct-value chip is keyed by `${profile.field}:${item.value ?? "__null__"}`. A genuine missing value arrives over the wire as `item.value === null` (the backend `_format_display_value` returns Python None for nulls, serialised as JSON null), so its key becomes `field:__null__`. If the same column also contains the ordinary string value "__null__" (a perfectly legal string after the backend's `.cast(pl.String)` in `_categorical_value_counts_expr`), that chip ALSO produces the key `field:__null__`. The two distinct chips then collide on the same React key.
findings.evidence: Backend: `_format_display_value(None) -> None` (src/haute/routes/_explore_service.py:119-120) and `_parse_categorical_value_counts` builds `ExploreDistinctValueCount(value=None, ...)`; the literal string "__null__" survives `.cast(pl.String).value_counts(...)` unchanged. Frontend: `profile.values.map((item) => (<span key={`${profile.field}:${item.value ?? "__null__"}`} ...>)` (line 370). When values = [{value: null, count: 3}, {value: "__null__", count: 1}] both yield key `field:__null__` -> React duplicate-key warning and unstable list reconciliation (one chip may be dropped/reused incorrectly across re-renders), even though both counts are legitimate distinct groups.

findings.title: computeGini re-derives Gini that the backend already provides in result.metrics.gini, on a lossy downsampled curve
findings.description: LorenzChart calls computeGini(curve, perfectCurve) to annotate the chart with a Gini value. But the backend already computes the canonical normalised Gini (_metrics.py:189 _gini, registered as 'gini' at _metrics.py:976) and ships it to the frontend in result.metrics, which SummaryTab.tsx:120 renders directly. The frontend therefore (a) duplicates a non-trivial metric the backend owns, and (b) computes it from result.lorenz_curve, which compute_lorenz_curve (_metrics.py:805-818) explicitly DOWNSAMPLES to at most n_points=200 unique indices via np.round(np.linspace(...)). Trapezoidal area over a downsampled monotone Lorenz curve under-estimates the true area, so the chart's 'Gini = X.XXXX' can disagree with the 'gini' value shown in the Summary tab of the same panel. The fix is to display result.metrics.gini (or a dedicated gini field) rather than recomputing.
findings.evidence: Backend: _metrics.py:224 area = np.trapezoid(cum_loss/total_loss, cum_weight/total_weight); raw_gini = 1 - 2*area; normalised by perfect_gini -> registered 'gini' (_metrics.py:976). Frontend LiftTab.tsx:364 rawGini = 2*trapArea(curve) - 1; LiftTab.tsx:367 return rawGini/perfectGini — same ratio mathematically (numerator and denominator both sign-flipped vs backend) BUT trapArea runs over the downsampled `curve` (>=200-point cap, _metrics.py:807-810), whereas backend _gini runs over the full per-unique-key aggregated points. SummaryTab.tsx:120 Object.entries(result.metrics) renders 'gini' with fmt(v). Two 'Gini' numbers for one model, derivable from the same payload, can differ.
findings.est_reduction: ~23 lines (delete computeGini at LiftTab.tsx:347-370 and the call/annotation wiring at 256/315-317), replacing with a prop carrying result.metrics.gini.
findings.behavior_preservation: Behaviour changes intentionally only in that the annotation becomes exactly the canonical backend Gini (eliminating the downsample-induced discrepancy). If exact byte-for-byte annotation must be preserved, this is a consistency bug rather than a pure refactor; either way the duplicate client-side derivation should go.

findings.title: DoubleLiftChart y-axis padding breaks for all-negative data: padded yMax falls below the true maximum, pushing the zero line and bars above the chart top
findings.description: yMax = allVals.reduce(max) * 1.1 and yMin = Math.min(0, reduce(min) * 1.1). The *1.1 'headroom' multiplier assumes the extremes are non-negative. When all decile values are negative (possible for regression targets / signed residual-style averages), multiplying a negative maximum by 1.1 makes yMax MORE negative than the actual largest value, so the data point lies above the plotted top of the axis. Worse, zeroY = yScale(0) is then computed for a 0 that sits above yMax: (0 - yMin)/ySpan > 1, so zeroY < marginTop, i.e. the zero baseline and every downward bar (drawn from zeroY for d.value < 0, lines 142/144) render above the chart's top edge / get clipped. Standard pricing diagnostics (frequency/severity averages) are non-negative so this is an unusual-input edge, but the code claims to support negatives (it has a yMin<0 zero-line branch at line 132 and signed-bar logic at 141-144), so the padding logic is internally inconsistent with that support.
findings.evidence: data = [{actual:-1,...},{actual:-2,...}]: allVals=[-1,-2]; yMax = max(-1,-2)*1.1 = -1.1; yMin = min(0, min(-1,-2)*1.1) = min(0,-2.2) = -2.2; ySpan = 1.1. For the largest value actual=-1 (>=0 is false) -> actualY = zeroY = yScale(0) = marginTop + chartH - ((0 - (-2.2))/1.1)*chartH = marginTop + chartH - 2*chartH = marginTop - chartH < marginTop. Bar top is a full chartH above the chart. Correct padding for the negative side would multiply the negative extreme outward (e.g. min*1.1 only when min<0, and pad the positive extreme by *1.1 only when max>0).
findings.behavior_preservation: N/A (bug report)

findings.title: Dead banding sub-condition in showColumnValuesTable is fully subsumed by !richNodeDetail
findings.description: showColumnValuesTable = !step.expression && !step.calculation && !richNodeDetail && !(hasRichBandingDetail(step) && hasRenderableBandingRows(step.node_detail)). The trailing banding clause can never change the result: richNodeDetail = hasPrimaryNodeDetail(step), and hasPrimaryNodeDetail returns true whenever hasRichBandingDetail(step) is true (it ORs hasRichBandingDetail in directly). Both predicates read the same step.node_detail and hasRichBandingDetail is literally `detail?.detail_type === "banding"`. So when hasRichBandingDetail(step) is true, !richNodeDetail is already false and short-circuits the whole expression; when it is false, the sub-clause is vacuously true. The `&& !(hasRichBandingDetail(step) && hasRenderableBandingRows(...))` term is therefore dead. It is also the ONLY use of hasRenderableBandingRows in this file (import at line 15), so removing the dead term makes that import droppable.
findings.evidence: StepCard.tsx:88 `const richNodeDetail = hasPrimaryNodeDetail(step)`; traceStoryView.ts:52-61 hasPrimaryNodeDetail ORs `hasRichBandingDetail(step)`; traceStoryView.ts:23-26 `hasRichBandingDetail` => `step?.node_detail?.detail_type === "banding"`. Thus hasRichBandingDetail(step) ⇒ richNodeDetail ⇒ the `!richNodeDetail` clause already gates out every case the banding sub-clause targets. Line 122 sub-clause never flips the boolean.
findings.est_reduction: 1 line of condition + 1 import symbol (hasRenderableBandingRows)
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior-identical: the removed term is logically implied by the preceding !richNodeDetail clause for all inputs, so showColumnValuesTable evaluates to the same value in every case.

findings.title: formatTraceValue emits a spurious 'full precision' title/aria-label for grouped non-integers (no precision actually hidden)
findings.description: formatTraceValue compares display (formatValue = _formatValue(v,2), which uses v.toLocaleString(undefined, {maximumFractionDigits:2}) and therefore inserts thousands separators) against full = formatResultValueFull(v), which routes to formatResultValue(v) with no precision and returns bare String(v) for non-integers (traceFormatting.ts:38) — NO grouping separators. For any finite non-integer with magnitude >= 1000 whose fractional part already fits in 2 dp (e.g. 1234.5), display='1,234.5' but full='1234.5', so display !== full and the function attaches title=`${context}: 1234.5` and ariaLabel=`${context}: 1,234.5 (full precision 1234.5)` even though NO precision is hidden — the strings differ only by the comma. Screen-reader users hear a misleading '(full precision ...)' announcement and a tooltip appears with zero added information. Separately, when precision IS genuinely truncated (e.g. 1234.5678 -> display '1,234.57'), the 'full' value is rendered without grouping ('1234.5678'), inconsistent with the grouped formatting used everywhere else in the trace UI.
findings.evidence: StepCard.tsx:22 `const formatValue = (v) => _formatValue(v, 2)`; formatValue.ts:28 non-integer path `v.toLocaleString(undefined, { maximumFractionDigits })` (grouped). StepCard.tsx:27 `const full = formatResultValueFull(value)`; traceFormatting.ts:45-47 -> formatResultValue(v) with precision undefined -> line 38 `return String(v)` (ungrouped). For v=1234.5: display='1,234.5', full='1234.5' => display!==full => StepCard.tsx:30-33 returns title+ariaLabel claiming full precision that does not exist.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: Same-name (on) join keys are never validated when base and join schemas are both known but share no columns
findings.description: commonColumnOptions returns [] whenever baseColumns and joinColumns have an empty intersection, including the case where BOTH parent schemas are fully known but simply disjoint. addColumnDiagnostics (line 350) early-returns when columns.length === 0, so addColumnDiagnostics("Same-name", onKeys, commonColumns) emits nothing. A same-name join (on: ["k"]) requires k to exist in BOTH frames; when the two known schemas are disjoint, every on-key is by definition invalid, yet the frontend produces no diagnostic. The user only discovers the bad key when Polars fails at run time. By contrast leftKeys/rightKeys ARE checked against the individual (non-empty) baseColumns/joinColumns, so the paired path catches this but the same-name path does not. The empty-commonColumns early-return conflates 'columns unknown -> cannot validate' (legitimate skip) with 'columns known but disjoint -> every same-name key is invalid' (should be flagged).
findings.evidence: commonColumnOptions (257-264): `if (baseColumns.length === 0 || joinColumns.length === 0) return []` then filters base by joinNames; for disjoint known sets this yields []. addColumnDiagnostics (344-350): `if (columns.length === 0) return`. Trace: baseColumns=[{a},{b}], joinColumns=[{c},{d}] (both known), on=["a"] -> commonColumns=[] -> addColumnDiagnostics returns immediately -> no "Same-name key a is not in the current upstream columns." emitted. The backend build_edge_join_kwargs (src/haute/_edge_join.py:157-212) does not validate keys against schema either, so this frontend guard is the only pre-run check.

findings.title: Blank-only same/paired key config emits two overlapping diagnostics ('need join keys' and 'rows cannot be blank')
findings.description: When config carries only blank key rows (e.g. on: [""], or leftOn: [""], rightOn: [""]), hasSameConfig/hasPairedConfig are true (length > 0) while hasSameValues/hasPairedValues are false (some(Boolean) on all-empty is false). Line 144 therefore fires 'Non-cross joins need join keys.' AND line 150's `[...onKeys, ...leftKeys, ...rightKeys].some((key) => key === "")` fires 'Join key rows cannot be blank.' for the same underlying state. The two messages are distinct strings so dedupe() (line 158) does not collapse them, surfacing two warnings for a single empty row. The in-app editor never persists a lone blank row (normalizeKeyRows trims it to []), but imported/decorator/API-sourced configs reach this code path with on:[""], so the redundant pair is user-visible for non-editor configs.
findings.evidence: onKeys for on:[""] is [""] (readKeyList keeps empty strings, lines 240-251). hasSameConfig = onKeys.length>0 = true; hasSameValues = onKeys.some(Boolean) = false. Line 144 condition (how!==cross && !hasSameValues && !hasPairedValues) is true -> push #1. Line 150 condition (some key === "") is true -> push #2. dedupe keeps both because the strings differ.

findings.title: CatalogTablePicker dropdown fetchers have no stale-response guard, letting a late getSchemas resolve repopulate the schema list for a catalog the user already left (and select an invalid catalog.schema.table)
findings.description: refreshCatalogs/refreshSchemas/refreshTables each fire an unguarded promise and unconditionally call setCatalogs/setSchemas/setTables on resolution, with no request-generation check or AbortSignal. Because the catalog/schema/table selects also re-fetch on every onFocus and on every onChange, a slow in-flight request can resolve after the user has navigated to a different catalog/schema and overwrite the now-irrelevant option list. The user can then pick a stale option, producing a wrong fully-qualified table string. This is the exact stale-response race that the sibling component CacheFetchButton (same directory's component family) defends against with statusGenerationRef/activeResourceKeyRef guards; CatalogTablePicker omits all such guarding.
findings.evidence: refreshSchemas(cat): getSchemas(cat).then((data) => { setSchemas(data.schemas || []); ... }) — no check that `cat` still === current `catalog`. Trace: (1) user picks catalog 'foo' -> onChange calls refreshSchemas('foo') [req B]; (2) user picks catalog 'baz' -> setCatalog('baz'), setSchemas([]), refreshSchemas('baz') [req D]; (3) req B (foo's schemas) resolves late -> setSchemas(foo schemas) while catalog='baz'. The schema <select> is disabled={!catalog} and catalog='baz' is truthy, so it is enabled and now shows foo's schemas. Selecting schema 'bar' fires onChange -> onSelect(`${catalog}.${dbSchema}.${tbl}`) building an invalid 'baz.bar.<table>'. The same pattern lets late getTables/getCatalogs overwrite their lists. Contrast CacheFetchButton.tsx:108-128 which guards every resolution with `if (activeResourceKeyRef.current !== requestKey || statusGenerationRef.current !== generation) return`.

findings.title: updateCell commits non-finite and partially-parsed values that the paste path rejects
findings.description: Direct cell edits go through updateCell, which uses parseFloat(val). parseFloat is lenient: it accepts trailing garbage ('1.2abc' -> 1.2) and returns non-finite values for overflow/literals ('1e400' -> Infinity, 'Infinity' -> Infinity, '-Infinity' -> -Infinity). Any of these are written straight into the entry value and propagated to onUpdateEntries (the rating config). The paste path for the SAME grid uses parsePastedNumber, which calls Number(trimmed) and guards with Number.isFinite, so it correctly rejects 'Infinity'/'1e400'/'1.2abc' with an error toast. Editing and pasting therefore disagree on what is a valid relativity, and the edit path can silently persist Infinity/-Infinity into the table.
findings.evidence: Line 192-193: `const parsed = parseFloat(val); const numVal = val === "" ? safeDefault : (Number.isNaN(parsed) ? safeDefault : parsed)`. parseFloat('1e400') === Infinity and Number.isNaN(Infinity) === false, so numVal becomes Infinity and is pushed at line 204 `next.push({ ...sliceKey, [rowFactor]: row, [colFactor]: col, value: numVal })`. Contrast parsePastedNumber (line 13-18) which returns {kind:'invalid'} for the same inputs via `Number.isFinite(parsed)`. ControlledNumberCell.onBlur passes the raw local string to onCommit (ControlledNumberCell.tsx:18), so arbitrary text reaches updateCell. Downstream tableStats (ratingTableUtils.ts:98) filters only isNaN, not isFinite, so Infinity flows into min/max/avg and StatsFooter renders '.toFixed(3)' => 'Infinity'.

findings.title: Label-based paste detection misroutes unlabelled numeric pastes when factor levels are numeric strings
findings.description: handlePaste decides whether a pasted block is a labelled table (header row + row labels) vs a raw value matrix by checking whether the first row's cells match colLabels and whether first-column cells match rowLabels. Rating factor levels are frequently numeric-looking strings (age bands like '18'/'25', vehicle-age bands '1'/'3', NCD years). If colLabels/rowLabels are such numeric strings, a plain unlabelled numeric value matrix whose first row/column happen to contain those same numbers is misclassified as 'labelled', so values are re-keyed by label-match instead of by position. The user's intended top-left-anchored paste is then written to the wrong cells (or partially dropped), silently corrupting the table rather than failing loudly.
findings.evidence: Line 163 `const labelledColumns = firstRow.slice(1).some(cell => colLabels.includes(cell.trim()))` and line 164 `const labelledRows = grid.slice(1).some(row => row[0] && rowLabels.includes(row[0].trim()))`. includes() does exact string compare, so when colLabels = ['18','25'] a pasted matrix like '18\t25\n0.8\t0.9' (first data row literally 18,25) sets labelledColumns true; if the first column also collides, labelledRows true, and the labelled branch (167-175) keys by `${rowLabel}\x1F${colLabel}` discarding the startRow/startCol anchor. The detection is purely value-based with no signal that the block is actually a header.

findings.title: Slice-match predicate and lookup-with-default are duplicated across build/read/update paths
findings.description: The same two pieces of logic are hand-rolled three times: (1) the slice-match predicate `Object.entries(sliceKey).every(([k,v]) => String(e[k]) === v)` appears in the lookup build (line 76), in applyCellUpdates (line 113) and (as a sub-clause) in updateCell.matchRow (line 195-196); (2) the 'read value with default' expression `lookup.get(`${row}\x1F${col}`) ?? safeDefault` is wrapped in valueFor (line 82) but then re-inlined verbatim in the cell render at line 284 instead of calling valueFor. Extracting a single `matchesSlice(e)` helper and using valueFor(row,col) at the render site would remove the repetition and keep the slice/default semantics defined in exactly one place.
findings.est_reduction: ~6-10 lines and three divergence points collapsed to one helper each
findings.behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: matchesSlice(e) and valueFor(row,col) are already the exact expressions inlined at the duplicated sites; substituting them is behaviour-identical (same key construction `${...}\x1F${...}`, same `?? safeDefault`, same String() coercion).

findings.title: Top-level TraceStep fields null_explanation / rename_info / expression_chain / taken_branch are never emitted by the backend and never read by any consumer
findings.description: The TraceStep interface declares five optional TOP-LEVEL fields beyond what the backend wire contract carries: taken_branch (line 48), taken_branch_index (line 49), null_explanation (line 50), expression_chain (line 51), and rename_info (line 52). The backend never serialises these at the step level. The Pydantic response model TraceStepResponse (src/haute/schemas.py:314-326) carries only node_id/node_name/node_type/schema_diff/input_values/output_values/column_relevant/execution_ms/expression/calculation/node_detail/row_lineage_type. The enrichment pass (src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py) writes the real equivalents INTO step.calculation instead: calc_dict['taken_branch'] / ['taken_branch_index'] (lines 1525-1528), step.calculation['expression_chain'] (line 1587), and step.calculation['original_name'] + step.calculation['rename_chain'] (lines 1252-1256, 1282-1287). A grep of the whole Python source (src/haute/**/*.py) for 'rename_info' and 'null_explanation' returns zero matches. On the consumer side, four of the five fields are read NOWHERE: step.null_explanation, step.rename_info, top-level step.expression_chain, and top-level step.taken_branch have no reader in any .tsx/.ts file (components consume only calculation.expression_chain at CalculationHero.tsx:158 and calculation.taken_branch[_index]). Only step.taken_branch_index is genuinely read, as a fallback at StepCard.tsx:237 (step.calculation?.taken_branch_index ?? step.taken_branch_index), so it should be RETAINED. The four others are dead on both the wire and the consumer surface. Note rename_info is doubly mismatched: its declared shape is {original_name; chain} but the backend stores original_name + rename_chain (different key, different location) inside calculation, so neither the field nor its key names ever appear on the wire.
findings.evidence: trace.ts:50 'null_explanation?: string | null' and :52 'rename_info?: {original_name: string; chain: string[]} | null'; backend schemas.py:314-326 TraceStepResponse has no such fields; _trace_enrichment.py:1252 step.calculation['original_name']=old_name, :1256 step.calculation['rename_chain']=chain, :1587 step.calculation['expression_chain']=enriched_chain, :1525-1528 calc_dict['taken_branch']; grep 'rename_info|null_explanation' over src/haute/**/*.py => no matches; grep '\.null_explanation|\.rename_info|step\.expression_chain|step\.taken_branch\b' over frontend/src .tsx/.ts => only references are the type decl and the guard parseTraceStep/parseTraceRenameInfo (guards.ts:813-814,828-833), which manufacture perpetual nulls; no component reads them.
findings.est_reduction: ~4 interface members (lines 48,50,51,52) plus the coordinated removal of their never-consumed guard parsing
findings.behavior_preservation: Removing taken_branch, null_explanation, top-level expression_chain, and rename_info from TraceStep is behaviour-preserving because no component reads them and the backend never emits them. KEEP taken_branch_index (read at StepCard.tsx:237). Because guards.ts:813-814/828-833 reference rename_info/null_explanation/expression_chain, removal must be coordinated with that file (a different bucket): the guard lines that construct these always-null fields would be deleted at the same time, with no runtime effect since the manufactured nulls are never consumed.

findings.title: PdpBarChart top-padding is wrong-signed for all-negative categorical PDPs, pushing the zero baseline outside the plot
findings.description: In PdpBarChart the y-axis top is computed as yMax = max(avg_prediction) * 1.1 and the bottom as yMin = Math.min(0, min(avg_prediction)). The *1.1 headroom only enlarges the visible range when the maximum is positive. When every categorical bar value is negative (e.g. a GLM / regression target whose predictions can go below zero — the codebase supports GLM models, see glm_coefficients/glm_relativities on TrainResult), max(avg_prediction) is negative, so yMax = negativeMax * 1.1 moves the top FURTHER from zero (more negative) instead of adding headroom. Then yMin = min(0, allNegative) = the most-negative value, and the computed zeroY = yScale(0) falls ABOVE marginTop (outside the plotting area). All bars are anchored at zeroY (barY = zeroY for negative values) and extend downward from a point above the chart, so they render partially outside the intended plot rectangle and the y grid/labels span an entirely-below-zero range. The bar-height geometry itself is self-consistent (verified: for v<0, zeroY + |v|/ySpan*chartH == yScale(v)), so this is purely a degraded/clipped visual layout, not a crash.
findings.evidence: yVals = grid.map(p => p.avg_prediction); yMin = Math.min(0, yVals.reduce(min, Infinity)); yMax = yVals.reduce(max, -Infinity) * 1.1; ySpan = yMax - yMin || 1; zeroY = yScale(0) = marginTop + chartH - ((0 - yMin)/ySpan)*chartH. Example preds=[-5,-2]: yMin=min(0,-5)=-5, yMax=-2*1.1=-2.2, ySpan=2.8, zeroY = marginTop + chartH - (5/2.8)*chartH = marginTop - 0.786*chartH (above the top edge). Bars then start above the plot. The sibling numeric PdpLineChart pads symmetrically (yPad = (yMax-yMin)*0.1) and has no such issue.

findings.title: Steps field eagerly clamps an empty input to 1, preventing clear-and-retype (inconsistent with min/max draft handling)
findings.description: Both Steps inputs are controlled (`value={steps}`) and their onChange is `onUpdate("steps", Math.max(1, parseInt(e.target.value) || 1))`. When the user clears the field to type a new value, `e.target.value` is "", so `parseInt("")` is NaN, `NaN || 1` is 1, and onUpdate immediately commits `steps = 1`. Because the input is controlled by that committed value, the field snaps back to "1" the instant it is emptied, so a user cannot delete the existing number and type a fresh one (e.g. clearing "21" to type "5" instantly becomes 1). This is the exact intermediate-edit problem the elaborate min/max draft state machine (activeRangeDraft + pendingConfigEcho) was built to solve, but Steps gets no draft handling at all, making the two number fields behave inconsistently. The backend already tolerates a missing/None `steps` (src/haute/_builders.py:859-861 defaults and clamps), so eager clamp-to-1 on every keystroke is unnecessary on the write path.
findings.evidence: L217-219 (standalone) and L283-285 (range) both: value={steps}; onChange={(e) => onUpdate("steps", Math.max(1, parseInt(e.target.value) || 1))}. steps = configField(config, "steps", "") (L67) is controlled, so committing 1 on empty re-renders the field as "1".

findings.title: Min/Max numeric draft handling is an over-engineered, fully-duplicated 4-field state machine
findings.description: To preserve in-progress numeric text (e.g. "2.0", "-", "0.") while the parent echoes the parsed number back into config, the component maintains a 4-field ScenarioRangeDraftState ({config, committedText, draft, pendingConfigEcho}) per field, a derived selector activeRangeDraft() with 5 branches comparing object identity/committedText/parsed-number equality, plus two near-identical 11-line resync effects (L93-103 and L105-115) carrying eslint-disable for set-state-in-effect, and helper closures setMinDraft/setMaxDraft/updateRangeDraft/commitRangeNumber. The entire apparatus is duplicated verbatim for min and max (every piece of state, every effect, every closure differs only by the Min/Max prefix). This is a lot of bespoke machinery and identity-tracking for a two-field decimal editor. A single small helper hook (e.g. useNumericDraft(committedText, onCommit)) parameterised over the field, or a simpler uncontrolled-with-commit-on-blur pattern, would collapse the min and max copies into one reusable unit and remove the resync effects. NOTE: behavior is currently correct and is pinned by a rich test suite (negative-zero, "0." preservation, cross-node clearing, same-value echo), so any refactor must keep those behaviors; the duplication and identity-comparison complexity are the cleanup target, not a logic change.
findings.evidence: ScenarioRangeDraftState type (L8-13), activeRangeDraft 5-branch selector (L30-46), two duplicated effects (L93-103 / L105-115) each with `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`, and parallel min/max state+closures (L71-91, L127-154). Grep confirms this draft pattern exists in no other editor — it is unique here, not a shared util.

findings.title: Artifact-load effect has no cancellation/staleness guard; out-of-order readJson resolutions can hide the metadata panel for the current artifact
findings.description: The `useEffect` that loads artifact metadata fires `readJson<ArtifactMeta>(artifactPath)` on every change of `artifactPath`/`sourceType` with no in-flight cancellation flag. If the user edits the Artifact Path quickly (A -> B), two POST requests to /api/pipeline/read-json race. Each `.then` writes `setMeta({ artifactPath, data })` tagged with its OWN captured path, and the render-time derivation `loadedMeta = sourceType === 'file' && meta?.artifactPath === artifactPath ? meta.data : null` (line 55) only displays meta whose tag matches the CURRENT path. When request A resolves AFTER request B (out-of-order completion), the last write leaves `meta.artifactPath === A` while the live `artifactPath === B`, so `loadedMeta` evaluates to null and the `ArtifactMetaPanel` (line 259) silently disappears for a path that loaded successfully; it only reappears if the component re-renders for another reason or the path is re-entered. The same staleness affects `loadError` (line 56). Notably the sibling `FileBrowser` in the same `_shared.tsx` (lines 179-205) guards exactly this hazard with a `let cancelled = false` cleanup, so the established codebase idiom is being violated here.
findings.evidence: Lines 109-123: effect body calls readJson(...).then(data => setMeta({artifactPath, data})).catch(...) and returns no cleanup. Compare _shared.tsx:179-205 which captures `let cancelled = false`, checks `if (cancelled) return` in both then/catch, and returns `() => { cancelled = true }`. Derivation at line 55 only shows meta when meta.artifactPath === current artifactPath, so a stale last-writer wins -> panel hidden.

findings.title: Clearing the run/version selection leaves a previously-mirrored optimiser_mode stale in config

findings.title: In-flight poll that resolves after unmount reschedules itself forever (post-unmount polling leak)
findings.description: The unmount cleanup effect only clears the currently-stored timeout handles; it does NOT delete the per-node entries from pollerState.current, and it does not invalidate configRef.current. Because isCurrentJob() decides liveness purely from `stateRef.current[nodeId] === state` (still true after unmount) and `configRef.current.jobs[nodeId]` (still the last-rendered, non-empty jobs map), an in-flight poll that resolves AFTER unmount passes the isCurrentJob guard and calls schedulePoll(state), arming a brand-new setTimeout. That timer keeps re-polling and writing to the store indefinitely after the component is gone.
findings.evidence: schedulePoll sets state.timeoutId = setTimeout(...) (line 180). When that callback is mid-`await pollFn(...)` (line 184) and the consumer unmounts, the cleanup at 306-310 runs `clearTimeout(state.timeoutId)` on the ALREADY-FIRED handle (no-op) and never deletes pollerState entries. The promise then resolves: line 191/214 `isCurrentJob(state)` -> `stateRef.current[nodeId] === state` is true (entry not deleted) and `configRef.current.jobs[nodeId]` is the stale last config (job still present), so it returns true -> line 215 `schedulePoll(state)` arms a new timeout -> next fire polls again -> infinite loop, plus onProgress/onComplete/onFail store writes after unmount. The existing 'clears all timeouts on unmount' test (useJobPolling.test.ts:590) uses mockResolvedValue so the poll resolves and schedules T2 BEFORE unmount, and cleanup clears the not-yet-fired T2 — it never exercises a poll still in flight across unmount, so the leak is untested.

findings.title: Redundant `lastProgressPublishedAt === 0` disjunct in queueProgress throttle gate
findings.description: The first-publish special-case `state.lastProgressPublishedAt === 0 ||` is fully subsumed by the adjacent `elapsed >= throttleMs` condition and can never independently change the branch outcome. It is provably dead within the boolean and can be removed.
findings.evidence: Line 142 computes `elapsed = now - state.lastProgressPublishedAt`. When `lastProgressPublishedAt === 0`, `elapsed = Date.now() - 0`, i.e. current epoch milliseconds (~1.75e12), which is always >= throttleMs (a few seconds at most, e.g. VISIBLE_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_MS = 1000). Therefore whenever the `=== 0` disjunct is true, `elapsed >= throttleMs` is already true, and the branch (immediate publishProgress) is taken regardless. Dropping `state.lastProgressPublishedAt === 0 ||` leaves behavior identical.
findings.est_reduction: 1 sub-expression (~0 net lines; simplifies the throttle gate to a single comparison)
findings.behavior_preservation: Identical: in every case where the removed disjunct is true the remaining comparison is also true, so the same publish-immediately branch is taken.

findings.title: matchCounts are mis-attributed to wrong breakpoint rows when boundaries are out of order or contain blank/invalid rows
findings.description: BreakpointGrid renders `matchCounts[i]` against breakpoint row `i` in the array's original order, but the caller (BandingEditor) computes matchCounts from `breakpointsToRules(...)`, which SORTS boundaries ascending and FILTERS out blank/non-numeric rows (and may append an extra open-ended band). The two arrays therefore do not align index-for-index whenever the user's breakpoints are not already in strict ascending numeric order, or contain a blank/invalid intermediate row. The displayed per-band match count is then attached to the wrong band, silently giving the user incorrect feedback while editing.
findings.evidence: BreakpointGrid.tsx:251-254 renders `{matchCounts[i] ?? "—"}` keyed by row index `i` (rows are shown in raw `breakpoints` order, never sorted). In BandingEditor.tsx:149-159, for `banding === "breakpoints"`: `const contRules = breakpointsToRules(bpRules, factor.rightClosed ?? true); return contRules.map(cont => previewRows.filter(...).length)`. bandingUtils.ts:233-296 `breakpointsToRules` does `bounded.sort((a,b) => a.boundary - b.boundary)` (line 252) and skips blanks/NaN (lines 243-249), producing rules in sorted, filtered order plus an optional appended open-ended rule (lines 287-293). Trace: breakpoints rows [{boundary:"30",label:"High"},{boundary:"10",label:"Low"}] -> contRules[0]=`<=10` (Low band), contRules[1]=`10<x<=30` (High band) -> matchCounts=[count(<=10), count(10..30)]. Grid row 0 ("High") shows matchCounts[0] = the Low-band count (wrong); row 1 ("Low") shows the High-band count (wrong). With a blank intermediate row [{"10","Low"},{"",""},{"20","Mid"}], contRules has length 2 so grid row 2 ("Mid") reads matchCounts[2]=undefined -> "—", and blank row 1 reads matchCounts[1]=Mid's count. The existing test (BreakpointGrid.test.tsx:291-306) only uses already-sorted numeric rows so it passes despite the gap.

findings.title: A `started` train response with a missing `job_id` is silently surfaced as a completed model instead of failing loudly
findings.description: In handleTrain the dispatch is: `if (result.status === "started" && result.job_id) { startTrainJob(...) } else if (result.status === "error") { completeTrainJob(...) } else { completeTrainJob(...) }`. The `&& result.job_id` guard means a response with `status === "started"` but a falsy/absent `job_id` does NOT register an async job — it falls through to the generic `else` and is stored via `completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as TrainResult)` as though training had finished. `parseTrainResponse` (frontend/src/types/guards.ts:1088-1089) validates `status` against `["started","completed","error"]` but parses `job_id` with `optionalNullableString`, so a `started`-without-`job_id` payload is a *valid* parse result and this branch is reachable. The stored object has no metrics/model_path (training never ran), yet getModellingPreview (useNodeResultsStore.ts:1098-1105) and TrainingActionsAndResults (TrainingActionsAndResults.tsx:202) only special-case `status === "error"`, so a `"started"` result renders the green 'Model trained — results in preview panel below' badge. This masks a backend contract violation instead of failing loudly, contrary to CLAUDE.md ('code should be allowed to fail loudly ... far superior to a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice'). The correct behaviour is to throw when `status === "started"` and `job_id` is missing.
findings.evidence: Line 140: `if (result.status === "started" && result.job_id)` → async path. Lines 146-149 `else { completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as unknown as TrainResult) }` catches `status==="completed"` AND `status==="started" && !job_id`. guards.ts:1089 `job_id: optionalNullableString(...)` allows null/absent. TrainingActionsAndResults.tsx:202 `trainResult && trainResult.status !== "error" && ...` → renders success badge for a `started` result that has no real output.

findings.title: Duplicate `else if (status === "error")` and `else` branches in handleTrain have byte-identical bodies

The only difference is the explanatory comment ('Immediate validation error' vs 'Synchronous completion'). Since both the error and the synchronous-completion cases call `completeTrainJob` with exactly the same arguments and no third (terminalStatus) argument, the `else if` predicate is dead — collapsing it into the single `else` is behaviour-preserving and removes a redundant branch. (Distinct from the known configHash="" staleness finding, which concerns store behaviour; this is purely the redundant control flow in the component.)
findings.evidence: Lines 143-145 and 146-149 both execute `useNodeResultsStore.getState().completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as unknown as TrainResult)` with identical args. `parseTrainResponse` restricts `status` to started|completed|error, so the `else` already covers `completed`; merging the error branch into it changes nothing observable.
findings.est_reduction: ~2 lines
findings.behavior_preservation: Identical: both branches invoke completeTrainJob(nodeId, result) with the same arguments; merging removes a redundant predicate without changing any call or its arguments.

findings.title: Switching utility files discards (does not flush) the pending debounced save, losing the last edit
findings.description: loadFile starts with `clearTimeout(saveTimer.current)` and the comment says "Flush any pending save for the previous file", but clearTimeout CANCELS the scheduled save without ever calling updateUtilityFile. autoSave (line 65-88) only persists by firing the 500ms setTimeout; there is no synchronous flush path. findings.title: Version <select> has no synthetic <option> for a persisted version, so the UI silently shows "latest" while config holds a different version

findings.title: detectGaps reports spurious/incorrect gaps when continuous rules overlap or nest (uses predecessor upper, not running-max upper)
findings.description: detectGaps sorts intervals by lower bound only, then in the loop compares each interval against its immediate successor using `curr.upper` (the predecessor's own upper) rather than the maximum upper bound seen so far. When an earlier-sorted interval has a wider/larger upper than a later one (i.e. the intervals overlap or one is contained in another), the comparison uses the narrower interval's upper and fabricates a gap that does not exist, or reports the wrong gap bounds. Because detectGaps is invoked only for `factor.banding === "continuous"` (hand-authored rules in BandingEditor.tsx:199), where a user can freely author overlapping/nested ranges, this surfaces a false validation warning directly to the user.
findings.evidence: Rules A: {op1:'>=',val1:'0',op2:'<=',val2:'100'} -> [0,100]; B: {op1:'>=',val1:'10',op2:'<=',val2:'20'} -> [10,20]; C: {op1:'>=',val1:'200'} -> [200,inf). After sort-by-lower order is A(0), B(10), C(200). Loop i=1 compares curr=B (upper=20) vs next=C (lower=200): `curr.upper(20) < next.lower(200)` -> pushes 'Gap between 20 and 200'. Actual coverage [0,100] U [10,20] U [200,inf) has its only gap at (100,200); the reported '20..200' is wrong. With B contained in A and C absent, a similar inner interval can even invent a gap where none should be reported at all. The bug is the use of `intervals[i].interval.upper` instead of a running max upper carried forward across the sorted list. BandingEditor.tsx:199-202 pushes these strings straight into user-facing warnings.

findings.title: breakpointsToRules silently emits a degenerate empty band for duplicate numeric boundaries

The resulting band can never be assigned, and no warning is produced, so a user with an accidental duplicate boundary gets a silently dead band.

Iter1 (prev=null): rule '<=10' label A. Iter2 (prev=10): rule '>10 && <=10' label B -> matchesContinuousRule(v) is false for all v (needs v>10 AND v<=10). Then open-ended '>10' label C. findings.title: defaultExpandedStepIds re-walks the same source-name/dependency-column traversal already implemented by targetDependencyStepIds + directInputSourceStepIds
findings.description: defaultExpandedStepIds performs the identical step walk used by the preserve helpers: find the target index, skip the target itself, skip steps after the target, then for each remaining step match sourceNodeNames first (else dependencyColumns) via stepCreatesOrModifiesColumn. targetDependencyStepIds (the dependency-column half) and directInputSourceStepIds (the source-name half) implement the same matching, and traceStoryPreserveStepIds unions them with the target. findings.title: ActualVsPredictedScatter re-subsamples to 2000 points, but the backend already caps the array at 2000 — the >2000 branch is dead
findings.description: ActualVsPredictedScatter contains a useMemo block that, when data.length > 2000, deterministically downsamples to 2000 points (lines 189-197), plus a footer that renders "Showing 2,000 of N points (sampled)" when data.length > 2000 (lines 274-276). However, the sole production data source for `result.actual_vs_predicted` is the backend `compute_actual_vs_predicted`, which is invoked with its default `max_points=2000` (src/haute/modelling/_training_job.py:1218) and already performs stratified decile subsampling so it returns at most 2000 entries. The only production render path is ModellingPreview.tsx:117, which passes `result` straight from the store. Therefore `data.length <= 2000` is always true at runtime: the useMemo always returns `data` unchanged, and the sampled footer string is never shown. The client-side `Math.floor(i * step)` linear resampling is also strictly worse than the backend's stratified-by-decile sampling (it would re-thin an already-stratified set with a naive stride), so even if it did fire it would degrade the distribution the backend deliberately preserved. The whole >2000 path is dead under the wire contract and adds an unnecessary useMemo + branch.
findings.evidence: Frontend: line 190 `if (data.length <= 2000) return data` then lines 191-196 build a strided sample; line 274 `data.length > 2000 ? 'Showing 2,000 of ...' : '${...} points'`. Backend: _training_job.py:1218 `actual_vs_predicted = compute_actual_vs_predicted(y_true, y_pred, w)` (no max_points override) -> _metrics.py:686-691 default `max_points: int = 2000`; for n>2000 it samples `per_decile = max_points // 10` per decile (<=2000 total), for n<=2000 returns all rows. Type contract: useNodeResultsStore.ts:65 `actual_vs_predicted?: { actual; predicted; weight }[]`. Net: `data.length` <= 2000 always, so the subsample branch and the 'sampled' footer are unreachable.
findings.est_reduction: ~12 lines (drop the useMemo subsample block; use `data` directly; collapse the footer to a single `${data.length.toLocaleString()} points` expression)
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving under the production wire contract: the removed branch never executes because actual_vs_predicted is always <=2000 entries. Only a synthetic caller passing >2000 raw points would observe a difference, and there is no such caller.
findings.behavior_preservation_note: If the team wants the component to stay defensively generic for >2000 inputs, the better fix is to keep a cap but not duplicate sampling logic; however given the backend guarantee, removal is the cleaner option.

findings.title: Stale pageIndex not reconciled when report prop shrinks; Previous button needs multiple clicks

The user must click Previous repeatedly (3 -> 2 -> 1) before raw pageIndex falls within range and the page actually moves. The Previous button is effectively dead for the first N-(pageCount-1) clicks.

Line 196 onClick={() => setPageIndex((current) => Math.max(current - 1, 0))} decrements raw pageIndex, not currentPageIndex. findings.title: Duplicated null-ratio bucketing across nullSeverity and nullPctStyle
findings.description: nullSeverity and nullPctStyle independently compute the identical ratio (nullCount / rowCount) * 100 and branch on the exact same thresholds in the same order: rowCount === 0, pct > 50, pct === 0, else. They map the same four buckets to a severity string and to a style object respectively. SchemaRow (lines 72-74) then calls both PLUS formatNullPct, computing the same ratio a third time. A single classifier (e.g. classifyNullBucket(nullCount, rowCount) -> 'empty' | 'high' | 'none' | 'normal') consumed by both call sites would remove the duplicated threshold logic and keep severity and colour guaranteed in sync (today a future edit to one threshold can silently desync the colour from the data-null-severity attribute).

SchemaRow lines 72-74 invoke formatNullPct, nullPctStyle, nullSeverity in sequence on the same (column.null_count, rowCount).

findings.title: Pagination/search gate keyed on report.column_count but slicing keyed on report.columns.length

The backend currently guarantees column_count === len(columns) (_explore_service.py:808-809 sets column_count=len(schema.names()) and columns=frame_stats.columns, one stat per schema name), so today they agree. But the component trusts two different fields for the same quantity: if report.columns.length > 50 while report.column_count <= 50 (any wire skew, partial payload, or future backend change where column_count is a declared/summary count), the table would render only visibleColumns.slice(0,50) and silently drop the remaining rows because the pager that would page to them is never rendered. The gate should be derived from the same array that is sliced (report.columns.length / filteredColumns.length).

Line 132 pageCount = Math.ceil(filteredColumns.length / SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE); line 135 visibleColumns = filteredColumns.slice(firstVisibleIndex, firstVisibleIndex + SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE). filteredColumns derives from report.columns (line 118). findings.title: Selection-reset effect round-trips feature names through join(",")/split(","), corrupting any feature whose name contains a comma
findings.description: featureKey is built as featureItems.map(f => f.feature).join(",") (line 51), and the reset effect then reconstructs the feature-name list inside itself via featureKey.split(",") (line 60) to decide the default/fallback selection. If any feature name contains a comma, the split produces the wrong number of tokens and the wrong substrings. Consequences: (a) names.includes(selectedFeature) can never match the real (comma-containing) selected feature, so the effect believes the selection is invalid and overwrites it; (b) setSelectedFeature(names[0]) (line 63) sets the selection to a corrupted prefix substring that does not exist in aveData, so selectedData (line 72-75) resolves to null and the user is stuck on the 'Select a feature' empty state for that dataset. Feature names are user-supplied data-frame column names (CSV/parquet headers), which are not guaranteed comma-free. The full featureItems array is already in lexical scope inside the effect, so the join/split round-trip is both the source of the bug and unnecessary: names could be computed directly as featureItems.map(f => f.feature) (comma-safe), keeping featureKey solely as the primitive effect dependency. The same pattern exists in the sibling PdpTab, but this bucket is scoped to AveTab.
findings.evidence: Line 51: const featureKey = featureItems.map(f => f.feature).join(","). Line 60 inside the effect: const names = featureKey.split(","). For a feature named e.g. "city, state", join yields "...,city, state,..." and split re-tokenises it into ["city"," state"], so names no longer equals the real feature set. Line 61: !names.includes(selectedFeature) is then true for the real name, and line 63 setSelectedFeature(names[0]) may assign a fragment like "city" that aveData.find (line 74) cannot match, leaving selectedData null (line 89 renders the empty state). featureItems is in scope at line 58, so the round-trip is avoidable.

findings.title: AveChart x-axis label truncation collapses distinct categorical levels sharing a 9-char prefix into byte-identical labels with no disambiguation
findings.description: truncLabel (line 149) shortens a label to maxLen via s.slice(0, maxLen - 1) + ellipsis, and the x-axis ticks call truncLabel(b.label, 10) (line 214), keeping only the first 9 characters before the ellipsis. Two distinct categorical bins whose labels share a 9-character prefix (e.g. "MERCEDES_BENZ_C200" vs "MERCEDES_BENZ_C220") therefore render the identical x-axis <text> ('MERCEDES_…'). There is no tooltip, title element, or other disambiguation on the bins/points, so a genuinely mis-calibrated bin (high avg_actual vs avg_predicted divergence) cannot be attributed to the correct level off the chart. This is the same defect class already catalogued for the backend static SVG renderer (render_ave_feature_svg / _render_dual_axis_chart in _charts.py), but it is a distinct, separately-rendered surface: the interactive in-app React chart, which has its own truncation width (10 vs the backend's 15) and no fallback hover text.
findings.evidence: Line 149: const truncLabel = (s, maxLen) => s.length > maxLen ? s.slice(0, maxLen - 1) + "…" : s. Line 214: const label = truncLabel(b.label, 10) -> for any label longer than 10 chars only label.slice(0,9) + '…' is emitted. Distinct backend categorical levels (e.g. produced by _ave_categorical_bins in _metrics.py) that agree on their first 9 characters map to the same displayed string. The <text> at lines 218-228 carries no title/aria/tooltip, so no other element distinguishes the two bins.

findings.title: Failed explore cancel leaves panel showing "Ready" instead of an error state
findings.description: In handleCancel's catch branch, failExploreJob is called with only (nodeId, message) and no terminalStatus. failExploreJob (useNodeResultsStore.ts:1056-1086) then stores the cached explore result with terminalStatus: null (terminalStatus ?? null) and error: message. After the job is removed from exploreJobs, the component's status derivation `status = currentExploreJob?.progress ?? currentCachedResult?.terminalStatus ?? null` resolves to null, so statusMessage(null, false) returns "Ready". The subtitle then reads e.g. "pricing | Ready" for a node whose cancel actually errored, while the only error signal is a transient toast that disappears. This is inconsistent with the startup-failure path (line 141-147) which passes a terminalStatus of {status:"error"} and correctly renders "Error". The stored error string is also never surfaced anywhere in the panel (currentCachedResult.error is read by no JSX), so once the toast clears the user sees a benign "Ready" for a failed operation.

Compare success path line 179 `failExploreJob(nodeId, cancelled.message||..., cancelled)` which yields "Cancelled".

findings.title: GPU-only params silently fabricate and then persist DEFAULT_PARAMS
findings.description: When the incoming params contain only the GPU flag (params = { task_type: "GPU" }), displayParams is {} so effectiveParams falls back to DEFAULT_PARAMS. The textarea then shows iterations/learning_rate/depth/l2_leaf_reg/early_stopping_rounds that are NOT actually part of the saved config (misrepresentation of persisted state). Worse, because `draft` is seeded from those defaults, the next commit bakes them in: toggling the GPU checkbox off runs handleGpuToggle(false) -> current = JSON.parse(draft) = DEFAULT_PARAMS -> onUpdate("params", { ...DEFAULT_PARAMS }), silently writing 5 hyperparameters the user never chose. Likewise a blur commits { ...DEFAULT_PARAMS, task_type: "GPU" }. This state is reachable from any node/pipeline config authored outside this panel that sets params to just { task_type: GPU }.
findings.evidence: L40 `const { task_type: _taskType, ...displayParams } = params` -> for params={task_type:'GPU'}, displayParams={}. L41 `effectiveParams = Object.keys(displayParams).length > 0 ? displayParams : DEFAULT_PARAMS` -> effectiveParams=DEFAULT_PARAMS. L42/46 draft and serialised = JSON.stringify(DEFAULT_PARAMS). L71 `current = JSON.parse(draft)` = DEFAULT_PARAMS. L72 disable branch `onUpdate('params', { ...current })` persists all 5 defaults. The DEFAULT_PARAMS fallback is meant for a genuinely empty config, but it also fires for GPU-only configs where the user has intentionally left hyperparameters unset.

findings.title: Feature-column derivation duplicated three times
findings.description: The expression `columns.filter(c => c.name !== target && c.name !== weight).map(c => c.name)` is written twice in this component (the Deselect-all onClick at L117-120 and the render IIFE at L131-133), and the equivalent filter `columns.filter(c => c.name !== target && c.name !== weight && !exclude.includes(c.name))` is also computed by the parent ModellingConfig (L118) to produce featureCount. findings.title: Candidate Curve chart suppressed when candidates have finite objective but non-finite decision_score (objective dashed line never shown)
findings.description: The entire 'Candidate Curve' SVG section is gated by `points.length > 0`. `points` is derived from `optimiserChartPath(...).points`, which contains ONLY candidates whose `decision_score` is finite (optimiserApplyHelpers.ts:154-164 builds `points` from `scoreCandidates`, i.e. `isFiniteNumber(point.scoreValue)`). However `optimiserChartPath` independently computes a non-empty `objectivePath` whenever any candidate has a finite `objective` (helpers:157-167). So when every candidate has a finite `objective` but no candidate has a finite `decision_score` (decision_score emitted as a NaN/Inf sentinel via the `__haute_type__: non_finite_float` wire encoding that formatValue/formatJsonSpecialValue explicitly supports), `objectivePath` is a valid path string but `points.length === 0`, and the whole chart block (including the objective dashed line, axes, and legend) is hidden even though there is renderable objective data. The gate should also consider the objective curve, e.g. `(points.length > 0 || objectivePath) && (...)`.
findings.evidence: OptimiserApplyDetail.tsx:40 `const { points, objectivePath, scorePath } = optimiserChartPath(displayCandidates)`; line 97 `{points.length > 0 && (` wraps the <TraceDetailSection title="Candidate Curve">. helpers:128 keeps a candidate if `isFiniteNumber(objective) || isFiniteNumber(decision_score)`; helpers:160-164 `points = scoreCandidates.map(...)` where scoreCandidates filters on finite scoreValue only; helpers:165-167 `objectivePath` is built from objectiveCandidates (finite objective) independently. Thus objectivePath can be non-empty while points is empty, and line 97 still suppresses the section.

findings.title: Selected-scenario score equation silently drops non-finite lambda terms, so displayed addends need not equal displayed score
findings.description: The selected-scenario callout renders a literal equation `objective <objective> + lambda <name> <value> ... = score <decision_score>`. The addends come from `selectedLambdaEntries = finiteRecordEntries(selected?.lambda_terms)`, which filters out any lambda term that is not a finite number (optimiserApplyHelpers.ts:18-21). The right-hand side `selected.decision_score` is rendered verbatim. If `lambda_terms` contains a non-finite term (NaN/Inf sentinel, which the formatValue layer explicitly models), that term is omitted from the shown sum while still being reflected in the backend `decision_score`, so the rendered equation does not visually add up (objective + shown_terms != shown_score). The plus-separated layout presents this as an arithmetic identity, so the silent omission is misleading rather than merely incomplete. Showing the term (e.g. as NaN/Infinity, consistent with formatValue's sentinel handling) would keep the equation faithful.
findings.evidence: Line 41 `const selectedLambdaEntries = finiteRecordEntries(selected?.lambda_terms)`; helpers:18-21 `finiteRecordEntries` keeps only entries where `isFiniteNumber(entry[1])`. Lines 80-92 render `{objectiveLabel}{selected.objective}` then `selectedLambdaEntries.map(([name,value]) => ...'+ lambda name value')` then `=score {selected.decision_score}` — the LHS omits any non-finite lambda term while the RHS shows the full decision_score.
